log-anonymizer.title: Privacy Shield Log Anonymizer
log-anonymizer.summary: Prepare troubleshooting and incident logs for review by masking recognized sensitive values while keeping useful technical context. Automatic redaction is a starting point for manual review, not proof of anonymity.
log-anonymizer.how_it_works: This browser utility scans text logs for supported identifiers and credential patterns. It replaces detected values rather than rewriting the event narrative. Stable labels help follow the same host or account through one processing run; generic labels reduce that correlation. Choose the mode according to what the recipient needs to know.
log-anonymizer.documentation:
Replacement counts describe recognized matches, not the number of people or all secrets in the file. Consistent labels preserve relationships within a run and therefore retain some information. A highlighted preview helps inspect changes; review the plain exported text too. A low count can mean that the log contains little sensitive data or that its format is not recognized.

The input limit is 50 MB. Free-text names, unusual telephone formats, bare opaque secrets and encoded data may be missed. Version-like numbers and other ambiguous strings can be redacted unnecessarily. Custom rules can overmatch; test them on a copy. Redaction is not encryption, a legal anonymization assessment or a guarantee that a log is safe to disclose.
log-anonymizer.examples:
Vendor troubleshooting

Keep timestamps, error codes and field names while replacing customer addresses and session credentials. Confirm that the remaining paths and messages do not identify a person.

CEF event review

When a supported extension label describes a credential, review both that label and its associated value. Unrelated extension fields should keep their meaning.

Line endings

The processing path preserves line structure; small-file loading retains original CRLF bytes for export. Pasting through another application may already have normalized line endings.
log-anonymizer.faq:
Does this find every name or secret?

No. It recognizes supported patterns and contexts. Unstructured names, unknown secret formats and indirect identifiers can remain. Manually review the entire result before sharing.

Can I share the replacement map?

The map contains the original sensitive values. Keep it private and separate from the anonymized log; only use it when you need to interpret stable labels.

Why are private IP addresses still visible?

The selected options can retain private address ranges. Review that choice before sharing internal network information.

Will processing upload my log?

The tool processes submitted text in the browser and does not upload it for analysis. Static page and worker files still load from CyberDat; extensions, clipboard tools and downloaded files are outside the tool’s control.

  • Offers stable or generic replacement labels, selected detection categories and custom regular-expression rules.
  • Provides a preview, anonymized text export and an optional replacement map. The map contains original values and must remain private.

How to Use

  1. Paste a representative excerpt or load a supported text file. Start with the smallest useful sample.
  2. Choose the data categories and label mode; add a narrowly scoped custom rule only when needed.
  3. Run the scan, inspect the preview and compare the event sequence with the original. Check unfamiliar fields manually.
  4. Copy or download the redacted log. Keep the original and replacement map separate from anything you share.

prompt-injection-detector.title: Prompt Injection Detector & Sanitizer
prompt-injection-detector.summary: Inspect retrieved pages, messages and documents for known prompt injection techniques before they enter an AI workflow. Findings support investigation; neither a clean result nor a sanitized copy establishes safety.
prompt-injection-detector.how_it_works: Prompt injection attempts to make an AI system treat untrusted content as instructions. A direct attack appears in a submitted prompt; an indirect attack can arrive through retrieved text, a document or a tool response. This detector uses deterministic heuristics rather than an LLM. It examines normalized text and bounded decoded fragments while reporting the location and reason for each recognized pattern.
prompt-injection-detector.documentation:
High severity signals a recognized strong instruction or technique; medium and low findings need contextual review. Findings are heuristics, not attack probabilities. Sanitization removes or replaces recognized passages and records changes. A modified document can still contain harmful instructions, ambiguous language or novel attacks. Never treat the output as a trusted system prompt.

The input limit is 20 MB. Large or highly obfuscated documents can be slow, particularly on some mobile browsers. Rules do not understand every paraphrase, language or intent; false positives and false negatives remain possible. Normalization can change text. This is a triage aid, not a complete prompt injection defense or a substitute for isolation and human review.
prompt-injection-detector.examples:
Retrieved document

Review a document that asks an assistant to change its task or conceal an action. The fact that it appears in a retrieved source does not give it authority.

Security report

A defensive report may quote an attack while explicitly rejecting it. Read the finding in context; quoted examples and negation can alter the appropriate severity.

Encoded content

An encoded fragment can conceal a directive. Decoding is bounded, so a clean result does not exclude other encodings or deeper layers.
prompt-injection-detector.faq:
Is sanitized output safe to give an agent?

It remains untrusted. Review the changes and residual content, and enforce instruction boundaries and restricted tool permissions in the consuming system.

Does no finding mean there is no attack?

No. Novel wording, unsupported languages and encodings can bypass heuristic rules. A clean result is not a safety certificate.

Can legitimate security writing trigger findings?

Yes. Reports can quote suspicious phrases or discuss attacks. Review quotation, negation and surrounding context instead of treating every match as malicious.

Does this call an AI model?

No. Analysis uses browser-side deterministic rules, not a remote model or external analysis API.

lotl-command-analyzer.title: LotL / LOLBAS Command Analyzer
lotl-command-analyzer.summary: Understand suspicious Windows command lines using a bundled LOLBAS snapshot and separate CyberDat heuristics. The analyzer reads commands as text and never executes them.
lotl-command-analyzer.how_it_works: Living off the Land describes the use of legitimate system utilities to perform attacker actions. The same executable can also be part of ordinary administration. This analyzer compares Windows command-line text with documented LOLBAS capabilities and adds contextual static signals. It helps form an investigation hypothesis rather than deciding intent from a filename.
lotl-command-analyzer.documentation:
A LOLBAS match identifies a documented capability and may include an upstream ATT&CK identifier and detection reference. CyberDat heuristics are shown separately and do not invent ATT&CK mappings. Severity reflects the recognized pattern, not a verdict that an event is malicious. Preserve the independent telemetry needed to assess intent.

The input limit is 5 MB. This release uses a fixed Windows LOLBAS snapshot; it does not include GTFOBins or provide general Linux shell analysis. New techniques, complex escaping and application-specific behavior may be missed. Legitimate commands can match abuse patterns. The snapshot date and commit are displayed in the tool; there is no live reputation lookup.
lotl-command-analyzer.examples:
Routine administration

A certificate utility can perform a legitimate management task. Recognition of the utility alone does not establish abuse.

Download-related alert

A command that resembles a documented download capability deserves review of its destination and the surrounding process chain. The analyzer does not contact the destination.

Encoded PowerShell

Supported encoded command text is decoded for static inspection. A decoding result is evidence to read, not a script to run.
lotl-command-analyzer.faq:
Does a high finding prove compromise?

No. A command can resemble a documented abuse technique during legitimate administration. Correlate it with process, account and network evidence.

Will pasted commands run?

No. The analyzer treats submitted commands as text, including decoded PowerShell fragments. It does not execute commands or contact destinations in them.

Where do the data and source come from?

The bundled Windows data comes from the LOLBAS Project. GPLv3 license and notice links, the pinned upstream source archive and the public CyberDat source are available with the tool.

Does no match prove a command is safe?

No. The available snapshot and static heuristics cover a subset of techniques. Missing or unfamiliar behavior still requires investigation.

mcp-security-checker.title: MCP Security & Policy Checker
mcp-security-checker.summary: Review Model Context Protocol configurations and tool descriptions before connecting them to an AI assistant. Static findings explain potential risks; the checker does not start servers or audit their implementation.
mcp-security-checker.how_it_works: MCP connects AI applications to tools and data. A client configuration can launch a local server or connect to a remote endpoint, while tool descriptions influence how an assistant chooses actions. This checker inspects supported configuration text and tool lists for risky settings, suspicious descriptions and policy conflicts. It does not verify the software behind an endpoint.
mcp-security-checker.documentation:
Findings identify static signals, not confirmed exploitation. A restrictive policy can make an otherwise intentional setting a violation. Recognized credentials are masked in supported report paths, but detection of an unknown or unconventional secret is not guaranteed. The tool does not automatically repair a configuration, probe a URL or install a package.

The input limit is 5 MB. Invalid or unsupported JSON must be corrected before meaningful analysis. Static text cannot establish runtime permission enforcement, package integrity, endpoint ownership or the absence of remote code execution. A clean report is not a complete MCP security audit. Unknown secret formats and novel description attacks can be missed; do not share confidential input or output without review.
mcp-security-checker.examples:
Broad filesystem access

Compare the configured directories with the minimum scope needed for the task. Access to an entire home directory can expose unrelated files.

New server package

A pinned package version makes a configuration more reproducible but does not establish that the package is trustworthy. Review source and operational controls separately.

Tool description review

Instructions to conceal activity or request unrelated credentials are warning signs. Their presence in a tool description does not make them authorized.
mcp-security-checker.faq:
Are all secret values hidden?

No. Masking is best-effort for recognized formats and contexts. Unknown secrets can remain, so inspect visible findings and exported reports before sharing.

Does the checker connect to configured servers?

No. It analyzes text locally and does not start MCP servers, fetch configured URLs or install packages.

Does passing a policy prove a server is secure?

No. A policy checks declared configuration against selected rules. It cannot verify runtime behavior or the server’s source code.

What should I do with invalid JSON?

Correct the syntax and confirm that the document uses a supported configuration or tool-list shape. Do not interpret a parse error as a successful security check.
